title: The “Constant Aggression” Strategy of Gryllus rubens (Orthoptera: Gryllidae) Males Reflects an Adaptation for Fierce Intrasexual Competition for Resources
content:
Many cricket species display overt intra-male aggression in the context of resource acquisition related to reproduction (e.g., burrows for mating). Various mechanisms have evolved to modify costly aggression behavior. In contrast to other cricket species, none of the previously reported mechanisms affected the aggressive behavior of flight polymorphic Gryllus rubens males when they fought conspecific rival males. Rather, and independent of morph, males displayed a constant high level of intra-male aggression, indicating high levels of competition for mating resources.


ABSTRACT

In many species, males have evolved overt aggression as a competitive strategy for resources. Due to the high costs that are associated with overt aggression, such as energy expenditure and the threat of injury or death, several mechanisms that regulate its performance have been observed. Gryllus field crickets (Orthoptera; Gryllidae) are a group of animals whose overt aggression in males is highly stereotyped and has been well studied. Previous work with various Gryllus species shows that male overt aggression can be mediated by several mechanisms that appear to be shared across species, such as suppression by experience (loser effects), reduced or delayed by life history trade-offs (dispersal capability vs. male aggression), or increased by motor activity that modulates hormonal state (resetting of aggression via flight behavior). Here, we studied the overt aggression of dispersal polymorphic Gryllus rubens males in staged male–male interactions. We tested the three mentioned regulatory pathways to determine how they might control male aggression. We predicted that male aggression would be similarly influenced by these mechanisms as observed in males of several other Gryllus species. In contrast to our predictions and previous work, however, we found that (1) male G. rubens were highly aggressive regardless of dispersal phenotype, (2) we did not detect a loser effect, and (3) the performance of motor activity prior to an agonistic encounter had a negligible effect on aggression. Our results suggest that mechanisms that regulate aggression are not consistent across closely related Gryllus species. Moreover, G. rubens males appear to have evolved a “constant aggression” competitive strategy that is likely shaped by their specific ecology, selecting for males to compete for access to burrows under natural conditions, which are a critical resource used for attracting mates and serve as refuge against predation.
